text: Then the Israelites set out and camped on the plains of Moab, across the Jordan from Jericho.
Balak son of Zippor saw everything Israel had done to the Amorites,
and Moab was terrified of the people, because there were so many of them. Moab was filled with dread at the Israelites.
So Moab said to the elders of Midian, "This horde will lick up everything around us the way an ox licks up the grass of the field." Balak son of Zippor was king of Moab at that time,

and he sent messengers to Balaam son of Beor, at Pethor on the River, in the land of his people, to summon him with this message: "A people has come out of Egypt. They cover the face of the land, and they have settled next to me.

Now come and curse this people for me, for they are too strong for me. Perhaps then I will be able to strike them down and drive them out of the land. For I know that whomever you bless is blessed, and whomever you curse is cursed."
So the elders of Moab and the elders of Midian went, taking with them the fee for divination. They came to Balaam and told him what Balak had said.
"Spend the night here," he said to them, "and I will bring you back whatever answer the LORD gives me." So the officials of Moab stayed with him.
God came to Balaam and asked, "Who are these men with you?"
Balaam said to God, "Balak son of Zippor, king of Moab, has sent me this message:
'A people has come out of Egypt, and they cover the face of the land. Now come and put a curse on them for me. Perhaps then I will be able to fight them and drive them out.'"
But God said to Balaam, "Do not go with them. You must not curse this people, for they are blessed."
The next morning Balaam got up and said to Balak's officials, "Go back to your own country, for the LORD has refused to let me go with you."
So the Moabite officials returned to Balak and said, "Balaam refused to come with us."
Then Balak sent other officials, more numerous and more distinguished than the first.
They came to Balaam and said, "This is what Balak son of Zippor says: Do not let anything keep you from coming to me,
for I will reward you handsomely and do whatever you ask. Only come and put a curse on this people for me."
But Balaam answered Balak's servants, "Even if Balak gave me his palace filled with silver and gold, I could not do anything, small or great, that would go beyond the command of the LORD my God.
Now stay here tonight, as the others did, and I will find out what more the LORD may say to me."
That night God came to Balaam and said, "Since these men have come to summon you, get up and go with them—but do only what I tell you."

versions.text: That night God came to Balaam and said, "Since these men have come to summon you, go with them—but you are to say only what I tell you."
versions.explanation: The Hebrew verb here is תַעֲשֶׂה ("you shall do"), not "speak." The contrast with verse 35, where the verb is תְדַבֵּר ("you shall speak"), is deliberate and should be preserved. The imperative ק֖וּם ("get up/rise") is also omitted.

text: So Balaam got up in the morning, saddled his donkey, and went with the officials of Moab.
But God's anger flared up because he was going, and the angel of the LORD stood in the road to oppose him. Balaam was riding on his donkey, and his two servants were with him.

versions.text: But God's anger flared up when he went, and the angel of the LORD stood in the road to oppose him. Balaam was riding on his donkey, and his two servants were with him.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew כִּי with the participle הוֹלֵךְ gives the reason and the ongoing action ("because he was going"), not merely the timing ("when he went").

text: When the donkey saw the angel of the LORD standing in the road with a drawn sword in his hand, she turned off the road into a field. Balaam beat her to get her back on the road.
Then the angel of the LORD took his stand in a narrow path between two vineyards, with a wall on either side.
When the donkey saw the angel of the LORD, she pressed against the wall, crushing Balaam's foot against it. So he beat her again.
Then the angel of the LORD moved on ahead and stood in a narrow place where there was no room to turn, either right or left.
When the donkey saw the angel of the LORD, she lay down under Balaam. Balaam's anger blazed, and he beat her with his staff.
Then the LORD opened the donkey's mouth, and she said to Balaam, "What have I done to you, that you have beaten me three times?"
Balaam answered the donkey, "You have made a fool of me! If I had a sword in my hand, I would kill you right now."
The donkey said to Balaam, "Am I not your own donkey, the one you have ridden all your life to this day? Have I ever been in the habit of treating you this way?" "No," he said.
Then the LORD opened Balaam's eyes, and he saw the angel of the LORD standing in the road with his sword drawn. So he bowed low and fell facedown.
The angel of the LORD asked him, "Why have you beaten your donkey these three times? I have come here to oppose you, because your way is reckless before me.
The donkey saw me and turned away from me three times. If she had not turned aside, I would surely have killed you by now, and let her live."
Balaam said to the angel of the LORD, "I have sinned. I did not realize you were standing in the road to oppose me. Now if this displeases you, I will go back."
The angel of the LORD said to Balaam, "Go with the men, but speak only what I tell you." So Balaam went with Balak's officials.
When Balak heard that Balaam was coming, he went out to meet him at the Moabite town on the Arnon border, at the very edge of the territory.

versions.text: When Balak heard that Balaam was coming, he went out to meet him at the Moabite town on the Arnon border, at the edge of his territory.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew reads "at the edge of the border/territory" with no possessive pronoun; "his" is an addition that makes the reference ambiguous (Balak's? Balaam's?).

text: Balak said to Balaam, "Did I not send for you urgently? Why did you not come to me? Am I really not able to honor you?"

versions.text: Balak said to Balaam, "Did I not send for you urgently? Why did you not come to me? Am I really not able to reward you?"
versions.explanation: The Hebrew verb כבד (piel) means "to honor" — it points to prestige and status, not merely payment. "Reward" narrows the sense to money and loses the note of honor that runs through Balak's dealings with Balaam.

text: Balaam answered, "Well, I have come to you now. But can I say whatever I please? I must speak only what God puts in my mouth."
Then Balaam went with Balak to Kiriath Huzoth.
Balak sacrificed cattle and sheep, and gave some to Balaam and the officials who were with him.
The next morning Balak took Balaam up to Bamoth Baal, and from there he could see the outer edge of the people.

versions.text: The next morning Balak took Balaam up to Bamoth Baal, and from there he saw the outskirts of the camp of the people.
versions.explanation: "The camp of" is not in the Hebrew, which reads simply "the edge/outskirts of the people." Trimming the added words also improves the rhythm of the closing line.
